questions.stem: Which of the following transition metals has the highest melting point?
questions.explanation: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all metals, about 3680 K, because it has a large number of unpaired d electrons that take part in strong metallic bonding. Zinc, copper and mercury have a filled or nearly filled d subshell and weaker bonding.

optionRationale.2: Zinc has a completely filled d subshell and a low melting point.
optionRationale.3: Copper has a filled d$^{10}$ configuration and melts much lower than tungsten.
optionRationale.4: Mercury is a liquid at room temperature.

questions.objective: Recall trends in melting points of transition metals

questions.stem: The most common oxidation state shown by the lanthanoids is
questions.explanation: Lanthanoids lose the two 6s electrons and one 5d or 4f electron to reach the stable +3 state, which is common to the whole series. States such as +2 (Eu) and +4 (Ce) occur only for a few elements.

optionRationale.1: The +2 state is characteristic of only a few elements such as Eu and Yb.
optionRationale.3: The +4 state is characteristic of Ce, Pr and Tb only.
optionRationale.4: The +5 state is not found in lanthanoids.

questions.objective: Recall the common oxidation state of lanthanoids

questions.stem: The spin-only magnetic moment of Mn$^{2+}$ (atomic number 25) is closest to
questions.explanation: Mn$^{2+}$ has the configuration 3d$^5$, with five unpaired electrons. The spin-only formula gives $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{5 \times 7} = \sqrt{35} = 5.92$ BM. Half-filled d$^5$ ions have the largest number of unpaired electrons in the series.

optionRationale.1: This is the value for four unpaired electrons, such as Fe$^{2+}$ or Cr$^{2+}$.
optionRationale.2: This is the value for three unpaired electrons.
optionRationale.4: This is the value for one unpaired electron.

questions.stem: Which of the following ions is paramagnetic?
questions.explanation: Ti$^{3+}$ has the configuration 3d$^1$ with one unpaired electron, so it is paramagnetic. Zn$^{2+}$ and Cu$^+$ are 3d$^{10}$, and Sc$^{3+}$ is 3d$^0$, so all three have no unpaired electrons and are diamagnetic.

optionRationale.1: Zn$^{2+}$ is 3d$^{10}$ and has no unpaired electrons.
optionRationale.2: Cu$^+$ is 3d$^{10}$ and has no unpaired electrons.
optionRationale.3: Sc$^{3+}$ has an empty 3d subshell and no unpaired electrons.

questions.objective: Identify paramagnetic ions from electronic configuration

questions.stem: The atomic radii of zirconium (Zr) and hafnium (Hf) are almost identical. This is mainly due to
options: the high ionisation enthalpy of hafnium
questions.explanation: Between Zr (4d) and Hf (5d) the 4f subshell is filled. The 4f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly, so the steady fall in size across the lanthanoids cancels the normal increase down the group. The result is nearly equal radii for Zr and Hf.

optionRationale.2: The inert pair effect concerns heavier p-block elements.
optionRationale.3: A diagonal relationship links elements of neighbouring groups and periods, not Zr and Hf.
optionRationale.4: Ionisation enthalpy does not control the equality of atomic radii.

questions.objective: Explain similar radii of Zr and Hf

questions.stem: In neutral or weakly basic solution MnO$_4^-$ is reduced to MnO$_2$. How many electrons are gained per MnO$_4^-$ ion?
questions.explanation: Manganese changes from +7 in MnO$_4^-$ to +4 in MnO$_2$. This is a gain of three electrons per ion. In strongly acidic solution it is reduced to Mn$^{2+}$, a five-electron change, and in strongly alkaline solution to MnO$_4^{2-}$, a one-electron change.

optionRationale.1: Five electrons are gained in acidic solution, where Mn$^{2+}$ is formed.
optionRationale.3: One electron is gained in strongly alkaline solution, where manganate forms.
optionRationale.4: Four electrons would take Mn from +7 to +3, which is not the product here.

questions.objective: Find the electrons gained by permanganate in neutral medium

questions.stem: 20.0 mL of 0.040 M KMnO$_4$ in acidic medium just oxidises 10.0 mL of a hydrogen peroxide solution. What is the molarity of the H$_2$O$_2$ solution?
questions.explanation: The balanced reaction is $2\,\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\,\mathrm{H_2O_2} + 6\,\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\,\mathrm{O_2} + 8\,\mathrm{H_2O}$. Moles of MnO$_4^-$ = 0.8 mmol, so H$_2$O$_2$ = 0.8 x 5/2 = 2.0 mmol. Dividing by 10.0 mL gives 0.20 M.

optionRationale.1: This uses a 1:1 ratio instead of 2:5.
optionRationale.2: This multiplies by 5 instead of 5/2, ignoring that two permanganate ions are in the equation.
optionRationale.4: This divides 2.0 mmol by 20 mL, the volume of KMnO$_4$, instead of 10 mL.

questions.objective: Do a redox titration calculation with permanganate and hydrogen peroxide

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Cu$^{2+}$ salts are coloured, whereas Zn$^{2+}$ salts are colourless.
Reason (R): Zn$^{2+}$ ions are diamagnetic.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Cu$^{2+}$ (3d$^9$) has an unpaired electron and a vacant position in the d subshell, so d-d transitions absorb visible light. Zn$^{2+}$ (3d$^{10}$) has a full d subshell and cannot show d-d transitions. Zn$^{2+}$ is indeed diamagnetic, but diamagnetism is a consequence, not the cause, of colourlessness.

optionRationale.1: Diamagnetism is not the reason for the absence of colour, so (R) does not explain (A).
optionRationale.3: The assertion is true: Cu$^{2+}$ is blue in water and Zn$^{2+}$ is colourless.
optionRationale.4: The reason is true: Zn$^{2+}$ has no unpaired electrons.

questions.stem: Match the alloy in List-I with its composition in List-II.
questions.explanation: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc (A-I). Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin (B-II). Stainless steel is iron alloyed with chromium and nickel (C-IV). Misch metal is a lanthanoid alloy with about 5 % iron, used in lighter flints and in making alloy steels (D-III).

optionRationale.1: This code interchanges the matches of A and B; the correct pairs are A-I and B-II.
optionRationale.2: This code interchanges the matches of C and D; the correct pairs are C-IV and D-III.
optionRationale.3: This code interchanges the matches of A and C; the correct pairs are A-I and C-IV.

questions.objective: Match common alloys with their compositions

right: IV. Iron with chromium and nickel

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. Chromium and copper have the configurations 3d$^5$4s$^1$ and 3d$^{10}$4s$^1$, respectively.
B. Mn$_2$O$_7$, in which manganese is in the +7 state, is an acidic oxide.
C. The atomic radii of the 5d elements are very close to those of the 4d elements of the same group.
D. The transition metals have low enthalpies of atomisation.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Cr and Cu are anomalous because half-filled and filled d subshells are extra stable. The highest oxide of a metal in a high oxidation state is acidic. The lanthanoid contraction makes 5d radii close to 4d radii. Transition metals have high enthalpies of atomisation owing to strong bonding, so D is wrong.

optionRationale.2: D is wrong because enthalpies of atomisation are high, and C is also correct.
optionRationale.3: D is wrong, and A and B are correct.
optionRationale.4: D is wrong, and this option omits correct statements B and C.
